content: Dead-in-bed syndrome refers to the sudden and unexpected death of young patients with type 1 diabetes who have no prior history of diabetic complications, particularly autonomic dysfunction. These individuals are typically found deceased in an undisturbed bed, which suggests that death did not occur during a convulsive episode. This phenomenon was first described in a case series involving 20 patients in 1991. Etiology Several potential causes have been proposed for dead-in-bed syndrome: Hypoglycemic unawareness, also referred to as hypoglycemia-unawareness syndrome. Ventricular dysrhythmia induced by hypoglycemia, which may result from QT interval prolongation during episodes of hypoglycemia. Autonomic dysfunction triggered by hypoglycemia, which can also lead to ventricular dysrhythmia due to QT interval prolongation. Diagnosis During autopsy, diabetic ketoacidosis may be investigated through biochemical analysis of vitreous fluid. Prevention Nocturnal hypoglycemia can potentially be prevented through the use of glucose sensors. Clinical practice guidelines from the American Diabetes Association recommend such measures. The MiniMed® Paradigm™ Veo system is considered one of the most effective tools for this purpose, although its cost-effectiveness remains uncertain. Additionally, closed-loop systems, often referred to as artificial pancreases, have shown promise in preventing nocturnal hypoglycemia according to systematic reviews.
